The Ku Klux Klan. A terrorist organization founded in 1866 by white Southerners determined to resist Reconstruction and Black political power. Operating through violence, intimidation, and murder, the KKK enforced a reign of terror against freedmen and their white allies, becoming the primary instrument of white resistance to emancipation and equal rights. Its ideology of white racial supremacy and methods of organized violence established a template for American extremism that persisted across generations.

The KKK was founded in 1866 in Pulaski, Tennessee, by Confederate veterans seeking to restore white dominance after the Civil War's end. It used masked night riders, cross-burning, whipping, and murder to terrorize Black voters and prevent their participation in politics during Reconstruction. The organization successfully suppressed Black political participation across the South through coordinated campaigns of violence and intimidation in the late eighteen-sixties and eighteen-seventies. The first Klan operated through cells with no central authority, giving individual chapters autonomy to decide targets and methods while maintaining plausible deniability at the leadership level. Federal suppression, notably under President Ulysses S. Grant, largely broke the organization's power by the eighteen-eighties, though it never entirely disappeared. Smaller cells persisted into the early twentieth century. The organization experienced a major revival in the nineteen-twenties, expanding beyond the South and incorporating anti-immigrant, anti-Catholic, and anti-Jewish ideology alongside white supremacy, bringing membership to an estimated four million at its peak. The second Klan explicitly modeled itself on the original, using the same symbolic imagery of robes and burning crosses to evoke historical precedent and legitimacy. The Klan served as the cultural model for American fascism and extremism throughout the twentieth century, with its imagery and tactics inspiring later hate groups and domestic terrorism. It became inextricably linked with the Civil Rights era, during which it attempted to suppress twentieth-century Black activism through renewed violence and the martyrdom of civil rights leaders.
